items.name: Behavioral modeling
items.title: Reinforcement-learning models of auditory categorization learning
items.claim: Ten reinforcement-learning models that separate what a learner knows from its pull toward repeating recent choices.
items.imageAlt: Real versus simulated learning curves for one mouse (GS027) under ten reinforcement-learning models, with each model's BIC difference from the best fit.

detail.lead: Mice learning to sort sounds into two categories often drift toward one response side for long stretches of training. This project asks what drives that drift, and builds the models so that each comparison answers one question.

sections.heading: Question
paragraphs: Is a learner's side bias something it learns from reward, or a reward-independent tendency to repeat what it has been doing? Choices alone can be fit by several of these stories, so the comparison has to be designed so the stories make different predictions.

sections.heading: Approach
paragraphs: A family of ten reinforcement-learning models assembled from interchangeable parts. Every model adds a few terms into a logit, turns it into the probability of choosing High, and updates what it tracks after the outcome. The models differ only in which terms enter and what gets updated.
**Baselines.** No learning (M1) and a noisy win-stay/lose-shift rule (M2).

**Two learning families.** The S family learns a value for every stimulus–action pair. The A family, the model of Collina et al. (2025) implemented as in their code, learns only how reliable each action is, with the stimulus mapping built in.
**Two add-ons.** R lets the learner drift toward whichever side has paid off recently. C is a choice kernel that captures reward-independent repetition, the piece the original model did not test.

sections.heading: Evaluation
paragraphs: Each model is fit to each mouse by maximum likelihood with several random starts, and learned values carry over from one day to the next. Correction trials update the model but are left out of the likelihood; the analysis is also run with them included.

Models are compared with BIC and group-level Bayesian model selection (Stephan et al., 2009; Rigoux et al., 2014). Following Wilson and Collins (2019), parameter and model recovery are checked on simulated data before any real-data result is trusted, and a result only counts if it holds in both the S and the A family.

sections.heading: Preliminary results
paragraphs: For one mouse (GS027), the model with the lowest BIC, A+C, does not reproduce the observed learning curves, while S0, A0 and A+R follow them more closely. A good score and a good account of learning are not the same thing; the group-level analysis is in progress.

sections.heading: My contribution
paragraphs: Designed the model family, implemented and fit all ten models, ran the model comparison and recovery analyses, and built the [interactive article](https://danceofthepkz.github.io/behavioral-modeling-thesis/auditory_categorization_learning/). Advised by [Prof. Joshua Goldwyn](https://www.swarthmore.edu/joshua-goldwyn); data from the [Geffen Lab](https://hosting.med.upenn.edu/hearing/) at Penn.

research.heading: Research
paragraphs: I am a senior at Swarthmore College majoring in Computer Science and Cognitive Science. My research examines decision-making under uncertainty at three levels: how animals learn to categorize sounds, how people assess risk when using AI systems, and how faithfully large language models reproduce the behavior of human populations.

I work with [Prof. Sukrit Venkatagiri](https://www.sukritv.com/) on human-centered AI safety. My senior thesis, advised by [Prof. Joshua Goldwyn](https://www.swarthmore.edu/joshua-goldwyn), develops reinforcement-learning models of auditory decision-making using behavioral data from the [Geffen Lab](https://hosting.med.upenn.edu/hearing/) at the University of Pennsylvania.
